title: The Silicon Sample Gets the Mean Right and the Variance Wrong
summary: Prompt a language model with a demographic backstory, ask it a survey item, repeat a few thousand times, and compare the aggregate to the real survey. The aggregate will often look good. Three preprints from the last four months,...
body:
Prompt a language model with a demographic backstory, ask it a survey item, repeat a few thousand times, and compare the aggregate to the real survey. The aggregate will often look good. Three preprints from the last four months, working across the General Social Survey, the World Values Survey, and the Survey of Public Participation in the Arts, all report the same thing: it looks good in exactly the place people check and fails in every place they do not.

That pattern is worth more attention than another round of "LLMs are biased." The failure is not noise, and it is not a bias term you could estimate and subtract. It has a shape. Simulated respondents are too similar to each other within a demographic cell and too different from each other across cells. That single distortion is enough to break most of the estimands a social scientist would actually want, and it breaks them in the direction that manufactures findings rather than suppressing them.

## Four years from promise to benchmark

The 2022 claim that started this was Argyle and colleagues' [algorithmic fidelity](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/political-analysis/article/abs/out-of-one-many-using-language-models-to-simulate-human-samples/035D7C8A55B237942FB6DBAD7CAA4E49): conditioning GPT-3 on sociodemographic backstories from real survey participants produced "silicon samples" whose response distributions tracked the corresponding human subgroups. The proposed use was modest and sensible — triage survey designs, pilot experiments, reach populations you cannot afford to field.

The correction arrived in pieces. Santurkar and coauthors built [OpinionQA](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v202/santurkar23a.html) and found misalignment between model-expressed opinions and those of sixty US demographic groups on the order of the Democrat–Republican gap on climate change. Bisbee and coauthors, in [*Political Analysis*](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/political-analysis/article/synthetic-replacements-for-human-survey-data-the-perils-of-large-language-models/B92267DC26195C7F36E63EA04A47D2FE) 32(4), found that ChatGPT's feeling-thermometer averages matched the 2016–2020 ANES closely while exaggerating the extremity and certainty of partisan division. Dominguez-Olmedo and Hardt, at [NeurIPS 2024](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2024/hash/515c62809e0a29729d7eec26e2916fc0-Abstract-Conference.html), evaluated 43 models on American Community Survey items and found responses governed by ordering and labeling biases — a pull toward the option labeled 'A' — with models drifting toward uniformly random answers once answer order was randomized.

What is new in 2026 is that the critique has become quantitative and cross-domain, at the same moment the technique has become market-research infrastructure. A July preprint, [*When Synthetic Users Fail*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.26348), runs one protocol across four models spanning two families and an 8B-to-frontier range, on two independent human-response corpora, benchmarked against non-LLM baselines fit on held-out human data. At the individual level no model beats the strongest baseline; on cross-cultural values every model falls well below it. On a segment-targeting task the models inflate between-segment gaps two- to fourfold, would send a team to the wrong segment in half the US cases and most of the cross-cultural ones, and invent segment splits with no counterpart in real people.

## Where the distortion lives

Write $d$ for a respondent's covariate cell — the demographic backstory you condition on — and $Y$ for the response to a single item. The population supplies a conditional law $p_d$ over responses; the simulator supplies $q_d$. The law of total variance splits the population's spread into a within-cell part and a between-cell part:

$$\mathrm{Var}(Y) = \underbrace{\mathbb{E}*d\big[\mathrm{Var}(Y \mid d)\big]}*{\text{within}} + \underbrace{\mathrm{Var}*d\big(\mathbb{E}[Y \mid d]\big)}*{\text{between}}.$$

Every reported failure is a statement about these two terms moving in opposite directions. [*Distribution-First Population Simulation*](https://arxiv.org/html/2607.18310v1), sampling characters from a 2,414-person World Values Survey pool, reports that independent agents pile onto a modal default: concentration on the modal response rises from 0.36 to 0.69, entropy falls from 1.46 to 0.77, 85% of units collapse, and the total-variation distance between simulated and real response distributions reaches 0.44. That is the within term shrinking. The two- to fourfold gap inflation is the between term growing.

My reading of why — this is synthesis, not a mechanism any of these papers claims to have identified — is that persona conditioning does not give you a sample from $p_d$. It gives you a sample from something closer to a *sharpened* $p_d$. Write

$$q_d(y) ;\propto; p_d(y)^{1/\tau}, \qquad \tau < 1,$$

the familiar tempered form. Sharpening is mode-seeking: it monotonically decreases the entropy of $q_d$ and drags $\mathbb{E}_{q_d}[Y]$ toward $\arg\max_y p_d(y)$. Two cells whose real distributions differ only slightly in shape but place their modes on different response options get pushed apart, because sharpening resolves a near-tie into a near-certainty. Preference optimization plausibly supplies the temperature — RLHF-style objectives reward the modal acceptable answer — and the persona instruction supplies the conditioning that makes the modes differ. The consequence is exactly the reported signature: entropy collapse within, gap inflation between.

This matters because the estimand in most of this literature is a between-group contrast. Take $\Delta = \mathbb{E}[Y \mid d_1] - \mathbb{E}[Y \mid d_2]$ and its standardized form $\Delta / \sigma_w$, with $\sigma_w$ the pooled within-cell standard deviation. Sharpening inflates the numerator and deflates the denominator. The bias is multiplicative at both ends, which is why a two- to fourfold effect-size inflation is unremarkable rather than extreme.

The second-order damage is worse. Standard errors computed from simulated data scale as $\hat\sigma_w / \sqrt{n_{\text{sim}}}$, and $n_{\text{sim}}$ is a budget line, not a sample. Both factors point the same way: $\hat\sigma_w$ is too small, and $n_{\text{sim}}$ can be made arbitrarily large for a few hundred dollars. The $t$-statistic is unbounded in your API spend. Any silicon-sample study that reports conventional standard errors over simulated respondents has reported a number with no inferential content whatsoever.

## Matching every margin and none of the structure

Even a simulator calibrated to reproduce each item's marginal distribution exactly can be useless, because a joint distribution is not its margins. Regression coefficients, factor structures, and cross-tabulations are all functionals of the dependence structure, and post-hoc marginal calibration touches none of it.

[*Not-quite-human tastes*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.30085) makes this concrete. Generating 277,470 silicon surrogates of Survey of Public Participation in the Arts respondents across models from three labs, the authors find a systematic positive bias toward liking — inflating ecological estimates of taste — and, more damagingly, that "the complex relationality in real taste structures is completely lost." Age–taste associations are attenuated, class–taste associations that sociology considers anachronistic are resurrected, and gender- and race–taste associations are caricatured. A simulator that got every univariate margin right and produced that correlation matrix would still be worthless for cultural sociology, whose entire object of study is the association structure.

There is a third nuisance term, and it is the one most likely to be silently ignored. Responses are not independent draws given a persona; they share a prompt. Helm and Priebe show in [*When prompt perturbations break your A/B test*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.27463) that under a statistical model of generative surveying with realistic perturbation structure, the sign test and the Wilcoxon signed-rank test are *invalid* — not merely conservative or slightly off. Semantically equivalent rephrasings of the item induce a shared component across all personas answering under that phrasing, and the classical tests assume an independence that this component destroys. They propose a permutation test that is valid under the model, characterize its power, and give guidance on splitting budget across personas, perturbations, and replicates. The operational reading: prompt phrasing is a random factor with its own variance component, and if you ran one phrasing you have $n = 1$ on the factor that may dominate your result.

## A numerical illustration

Take a five-point item and two segments with plausible human distributions:

$$p_A = (.10, .20, .35, .25, .10), \qquad p_B = (.06, .14, .30, .30, .20).$$

Means are $3.05$ and $3.44$; within-segment standard deviations are $1.117$ and $1.134$; pooled $\sigma_w = 1.126$. So $\Delta = 0.39$ and Cohen's $d = 0.35$ — a real but modest difference, the sort of thing a survey would need a few thousand respondents to pin down.

Now apply the sharpening map with $\tau = 0.35$, so $q \propto p^{2.857}$:

$$q_A = (.017, .123, .610, .233, .017), \qquad q_B = (.004, .047, .410, .410, .129).$$

Simulated means are $3.11$ and $3.61$; standard deviations fall to $0.693$ and $0.782$, pooled $0.739$. The gap widens to $\Delta = 0.50$ and $d = 0.68$ — a $1.97\times$ inflation of the standardized effect from a single parameter, landing squarely inside the two- to fourfold band the benchmark reports. Segment A's entropy drops from $1.50$ to $1.04$ nats and its modal mass rises from $0.35$ to $0.61$, which is the same order as the $1.46 \to 0.77$ and $0.36 \to 0.69$ moves reported on real WVS data. One knob reproduces the published collapse to roughly the right magnitude, which is at least suggestive that the phenomenon has one dominant cause.

The diagnostic that follows is the one I would run before trusting any synthetic panel:

```python
import numpy as np
def cell_report(p_real, p_sim):           # both (n_cells, n_options), rows sum to 1
    H = lambda p: -(p * np.log(p + 1e-12)).sum(-1)
    tv = 0.5 * np.abs(p_real - p_sim).sum(-1)
    y = np.arange(p_real.shape[1]) + 1.0
    mu_r, mu_s = p_real @ y, p_sim @ y
    var = lambda p, m: p @ (y**2) - m**2
    return {
        "entropy_ratio": (H(p_sim) / H(p_real)).mean(),      # want ~1, expect <1
        "tv_per_cell":   tv.mean(),                          # want ~0, expect ~0.3-0.5
        "within_ratio":  (var(p_sim, mu_s) / var(p_real, mu_r)).mean(),
        "between_ratio": mu_s.var() / mu_r.var(),            # want ~1, expect >>1
    }
Two numbers, `within_ratio` well below one and `between_ratio` well above it, are the fingerprint. If you see them, no amount of marginal reweighting will rescue a between-group analysis.
```

## What to do instead

Stop validating on aggregate agreement. Marginal fit is a necessary condition that costs the simulator almost nothing to satisfy and tells you almost nothing. Validate on the estimand your paper actually reports: if the claim is a regression coefficient, benchmark the coefficient against held-out human data; if it is a subgroup ranking, check whether the ranking survives.

Never compute standard errors from simulated respondents alone. The principled alternative exists and is well developed. Broska, Howes, and van Loon's [mixed subjects design](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1177/00491241251326865) treats LLM responses as potentially informative observations with human subjects as gold standard, extends prediction-powered inference to this setting, defines a PPI correlation as a measure of interchangeability, and derives an effective sample size you can use for power analysis and for choosing the optimal human/LLM mix. Hullman, Broska, Sun, and Shaw's [framework paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.15785) draws the line that matters: heuristic partial-replication arguments are adequate for exploratory work, statistical calibration against a human sample is required for confirmatory claims. That distinction should be a reviewing standard.

Randomize answer order and report the flip rate. Run several semantically equivalent phrasings and use a test that is valid under perturbation, not the sign test. And take contamination seriously — GSS, WVS, and ANES are all in the pretraining corpus, so agreement on them is ambiguous between knowing the population and recalling the file. The distribution-first paper takes this seriously enough to include a placebo-controlled memorization attack and an anonymized national-election backtest, and finds aggregate strength surviving while subgroup and individual claims are contaminated by recall and underdetermination. Benchmarks without a contamination control should be read as upper bounds.

## What is not settled

The negative results characterize one protocol: demographic prompting of instruction-tuned chat models. Fine-tuning on survey microdata, or the distribution-first recipe of modeling the population distribution once and assigning it to grounded characters, is a different regime, and it is not yet clear whether it fixes the dependence structure or only the margins.

My sharpening account has a real problem, and I would rather flag it than smooth it over. Dominguez-Olmedo and Hardt found models trending toward *uniform* responses once ordering bias was removed — maximum entropy, the opposite of collapse. The 2026 work finds minimum-entropy pile-up. These cannot both be the general behavior. The plausible reconciliations are that base and heavily preference-tuned models differ qualitatively, or that the two protocols elicit different things, but as far as I can tell nobody has run the experiment that separates them. Until someone does, "LLMs have the wrong entropy" is better supported than any specific claim about which direction.

Prediction-powered inference is the right machinery, and it is worth being clear about what it does not deliver. PPI restores valid inference by anchoring on human data; its benefit is a variance reduction whose size is governed by the human–LLM correlation. When that correlation is low — which is precisely the regime these benchmarks document for individual-level prediction — the effective sample size gain approaches nothing. PPI does not enable the use case that motivated the field, which was surveying without surveying. It converts a validity problem into a cost problem, honestly.

The construct-validity question has barely been asked. No one has established that a persona-conditioned generation measures the same latent quantity a survey item measures in a human. Absent that, distributional agreement is a coincidence of outputs, not evidence about a shared construct — and the sociologists whose association structures vanish in the silicon data are the ones with standing to say so.

Finally, the ethical geometry is uncomfortable. The strongest argument for simulated respondents has always been access to populations that are expensive or impossible to field, and the cross-cultural results are where fidelity is worst. The method fails hardest exactly where it was supposed to help most, which is an argument against deploying it there rather than an argument for more prompting.

## Further reading

- Argyle et al., *Out of One, Many: Using Language Models to Simulate Human Samples*, Political Analysis, 2023. [cambridge.org](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/political-analysis/article/abs/out-of-one-many-using-language-models-to-simulate-human-samples/035D7C8A55B237942FB6DBAD7CAA4E49) — the origin of "algorithmic fidelity" and silicon samples; read it for how carefully hedged the original claim was compared to what it became.
- Santurkar, Durmus, Ladhak, Lee, Liang, Hashimoto, *Whose Opinions Do Language Models Reflect?*, ICML 2023, PMLR 202:29971–30004. [proceedings.mlr.press](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v202/santurkar23a.html) — OpinionQA; the first systematic subgroup-alignment measurement.
- Bisbee, Clinton, Dorff, Kenkel, Larson, *Synthetic Replacements for Human Survey Data? The Perils of Large Language Models*, Political Analysis 32(4):401–416, 2024. [cambridge.org](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/political-analysis/article/synthetic-replacements-for-human-survey-data-the-perils-of-large-language-models/B92267DC26195C7F36E63EA04A47D2FE) — right means, exaggerated division; the cleanest early statement of the variance problem.
- Dominguez-Olmedo, Hardt, *Questioning the Survey Responses of Large Language Models*, NeurIPS 2024. [proceedings.neurips.cc](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2024/hash/515c62809e0a29729d7eec26e2916fc0-Abstract-Conference.html) — 43 models, ordering bias, and the uniform-response finding that complicates every collapse story including mine.
- *When Synthetic Users Fail: A Cross-Domain Benchmark of LLM-Simulated Human Survey Responses*, arXiv:2607.26348, July 2026. [arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.26348) — the benchmark to cite; note especially the non-LLM baselines, which almost nobody else includes.
- *Distribution-First Population Simulation: Collapse, Calibration, and Recall in Non-WEIRD LLM Persona Modeling*, arXiv:2607.18310, July 2026. [arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/html/2607.18310v1) — the collapse numbers, the memorization placebo, and a constructive alternative.
- *Not-quite-human tastes: the stylized omnivorousness of LLM survey surrogates*, arXiv:2606.30085, June 2026. [arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.30085) — 277,470 surrogates; the best demonstration that association structure, not margins, is what breaks.
- Helm, Priebe, *When prompt perturbations break your A/B test: A valid statistical test for generative surveying*, arXiv:2605.27463, May 2026. [arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.27463) — sign and Wilcoxon tests shown invalid, with a permutation test and budget guidance to replace them.
- Hullman, Broska, Sun, Shaw, *This human study did not involve human subjects: Validating LLM simulations as behavioral evidence*, arXiv:2602.15785, 2026. [arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.15785) — the exploratory/confirmatory distinction that should govern reviewing; see also the authors' [summary post](https://statmodeling.stat.columbia.edu/2025/12/19/validating-language-models-as-study-participants-how-its-being-done-why-it-fails-and-what-works-instead/).
- Broska, Howes, van Loon, *The Mixed Subjects Design: Treating Large Language Models as Potentially Informative Observations*, Sociological Methods & Research, 2025. [journals.sagepub.com](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1177/00491241251326865) — PPI correlation, effective sample size, and power analysis for human/LLM mixes; the constructive paper in this literature.
